subject: What Danny Welbeck could offer Chelsea: Goals, channel runs and vital know-how
body:
As Chelsea prepare to buy a striker for the seventh straight summer, Danny Welbeck has emerged as a surprise candidate to be that man.

The 35-year-old is into the final year of his contract with Brighton & Hove Albion and, off the back of his two best-ever Premier League seasons (10 goals in 2024-25, then 13), he might offer new manager Xabi Alonso some solutions to Chelsea’s seemingly perennial No 9 problem.

Welbeck is at the opposite end of the age scale to Liam Delap, the now 23-year-old Manchester City academy graduate signed from relegated Ipswich Town last summer. A young Delap offered raw potential, physical quality and respectable goals numbers. The same can be said for Marc Guiu, bought as an 18-year-old in 2024, and Nicolas Jackson, now 25, who joined the year before him.

body: Plus: Opinion from Jemima Kelly, and why it pays to kiss up and kick down ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Hannah Rock Editor, FT Edit ‌ ‌ July 13 2026 Good afternoon, here is today’s edition of FT Edit, your daily slice of the FT. For much of the last century, Citi was one of Wall Street’s most prestigious institutions. The bank helped finance wars, aided US companies operating abroad and managed the money of middle-class Americans at home. Then it all went wrong. In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crash, Citi received the largest bailout of any Wall Street bank, sparking its decline from largest major US lender to the smallest. Can Citigroup boss Jane Fraser — unassuming, charming, ruthless — turn it around? And how far is she willing to go? Read the story ➼ P.S. The number of young people who are “Neet” — not in education, employment or training — has topped 1mn in the UK, and parents are being forced to step in. But where’s the line between support and mollycoddling? subject: World Cup semi-finals bracket predictions: Picking the winners and key players for final four
body:
After 100 matches at World Cup 2026 there are four teams left standing.

Kylian Mbappe and France overcame Morocco, Lamine Yamal and Spain eased past Belgium, Jude Bellingham helped England eliminate Erling Haaland’s Norway in extra-time. Lionel Messi and defending champions Argentina became the last team into the semi-finals by defeating Switzerland, with the help of a stunning extra-time strike from Julian Alvarez.

The ties will take place on Tuesday and Wednesday with the final taking place on Sunday at MetLife Stadium (and a bronze-medal match the day before in Miami).

subject: Spreading the wealth in America
body: Plus: AI is not enough to arrest China’s decline ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser SPREADING THE WEALTH IN AMERICA Ursula Milton Commissioning Editor, FT Opinion ‌ ‌ July 13 2026 The winner-takes-all AI economy is exacerbating worries about uneven wealth distribution in America, writes Rana Foroohar. That’s one reason why the US president has launched “Trump accounts”. These give children born during his second term a one-off $1,000 to invest in an S&P 500 tracker fund. The results will in no way be transformative, Rana notes, but the fact that even Trump is concerned about the issue speaks to the larger debate in the US over “predistribution” — as opposed to the “redistribution” — of wealth. If predistribution is to work, she concludes, it must be about spreading wealth in a bigger and much more sustainable way. Ruchir Sharma suggests China’s vaunted AI prowess conceals deep rot elsewhere in its economy. The new technology is not providing a big enough boost to overcome other forces weighing on the country, he says. These include a shrinking workforce, rising indebtedness, the revival of state meddling and the resulting exodus of capital and people. Elsewhere, Jemima Kelly spots an unlikely internet hero emerging from nowhere: Hunter Biden. He may be a nepo baby, Jemima says, “but he manages to come across like a real, flawed and often quite funny human being”. And Martin Sandbu writes that Ireland’s hardest task as it takes on the rotating presidency of the EU will be to advance talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget. ‌ ‌ Thanks for reading. subject: US-Iran ceasefire teeters
body: Plus, bumper investment banking gains and UK council homes ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Irwin Cruz Digital Editor ‌ ‌ July 13 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * US launches another round of strikes on Iran as ceasefire teeters * Wall Street feasts on fees from SpaceX IPO and mega-mergers * Andy Burnham’s big plan to build council houses * Jane Fraser’s ruthless remake of Citigroup You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast. ‌ We begin in the Middle East, where the US has carried out a fifth round of strikes on Iran, sparking retaliation from Tehran, as hostilities escalated over control of the Strait of Hormuz. The latest: US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, carried out two rounds of strikes on Sunday in order to “degrade Iran’s ability to continue attacking international shipping flowing through the Strait of Hormuz”. The strikes hit dozens of targets, including “military air-defence systems, coastal radar sites, missile and drone capabilities, and small boats and involved fighter jets, warships, one-way attack aerial drones and, for the first time, one-way attack sea drones”, Centcom said. Centcom said its strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at a commercial vessel, and said US forces had intercepted an Iranian cruise missile and drone. In response, the IRGC said its forces had carried out multiple rounds of retaliatory operations overnight, targeting US military bases, hitting missile depots and fuel storage tanks in Jordan, a helicopter facility, electronic warfare aircraft and a drone command and control centre in Bahrain and a Patriot air defence system in Kuwait. Why it matters: The spate of tit-for-tat exchanges within the past week between Washington and Tehran risks a return to full-scale war, with a ceasefire agreement between the sides on the verge of collapse. US President Donald Trump has struggled to negotiate an end to the violence, which has damaged his approval ratings, strained relations with allies and hit voters with higher petrol prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Market reaction: Oil prices rose after the latest exchanges, with Brent, the international benchmark, up 4 per cent in early Asian trading to $79 a barrel. Futures for the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent and 0.5 per cent, respectively. The dollar strengthened 0.2 per cent against a basket of key trading partners. * Iran’s gambit: The Islamic republic remains defiant and convinced it has the advantage by closing the strait. But the risk is that it overplays its hand. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Ukraine war: French President Emmanuel Macron hosts a meeting in Paris of the “coalition of the willing”, set up for European allies to discuss security guarantees for Kyiv. * Energy markets: Opec publishes its monthly oil report. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. Wall Street banks this week are set to report a 27 per cent gain from investment banking fees for the second quarter year on year, according to forecasts, fuelled by SpaceX’s blockbuster stock market listing and a resurgence of mega-mergers. 2. Andy Burnham, the prime minister-in-waiting, has promised Britain’s “biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”. But while his message is radical, his language is loose, leaving major questions over the plan’s scale and likely cost. * Policy plans: Burnham is exploring holding an expanded Budget this autumn, combining the fiscal statement with a departmental spending review. 3. Europe imported more liquefied natural gas from Russia’s leading LNG project than ever before in the first half of 2026, absorbing nearly all of the Siberian facility’s output months before an EU ban on Russian gas imports comes into effect. The figures underline the crucial role the continent still plays in keeping Russia’s flagship energy facility running. 4. Companies from Silicon Valley to Europe are turning to Chinese AI models as they try to cut the cost of using the technology and reduce reliance on US frontier labs. Here are the groups that have made the switch, drawn by cheaper and more capable models that are, in some cases, easier to run on their own infrastructure. * Opinion: China’s vaunted AI prowess is concealing deep rot elsewhere in its economy, writes Ruchir Sharma. 5. Exclusive: Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has called on JPMorgan Chase boss Jamie Dimon to say whether he lobbied the UK government against a tax on bankers’ bonuses on the advice of child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Read the full story. THE BIG READ © FT montage/Bloomberg Jane Fraser, Citi’s Scottish-born chief executive, has reorganised the 214-year-old bank, selling assets and shedding tens of thousands of jobs while making controversial new hires and cultivating relations with the Trump administration. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which owns Citi shares, says that while there was “a lot of disbelief” that Fraser would succeed where her predecessors failed in reinventing the bank, “it looks like she’s done a fantastic job”. But some employees fret over the institution’s aggressive new culture, worrying that it will make it more difficult for Citi to deal with the legacy of past errors. Investors, analysts and executives at rival institutions, on the other hand, say that Citi is clearly a better-functioning bank under Fraser. But they add that she now needs to show she can grow the lender, not just fix it. Read Akila Quinio’s deep dive into Fraser’s ruthless remake of Citigroup. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * ‘Trump accounts’: How does one spread America’s wealth, asks Rana Foroohar. Is the answer pre-distribution rather than redistribution? * Extreme weather: More than 2,700 deaths across England and Wales have been linked to the record-breaking heatwaves that hit the UK in May and June. * ‘Confusing’ signals: Deep splits of opinion on the Bank of England’s rate-setting committee are making it harder to rebuild the central bank’s credibility. * Ukraine overhaul: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that he will replace the country’s prime minister and shake up his cabinet. CHART OF THE DAY Private equity’s biggest players are driving a fundraising revival that has left smaller firms trailing, with the market seized by a winner-takes-all dynamic. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . subject: Invitation to connect with Apple
body: Hi Umair, We recently invited you to talk with us about opportunities at Apple, but we haven't yet heard back from you. If you're still interested, here are the details. Event Details Apple Retail - Singapore - Phone Screening 13-Jul-2026 - 17-Jul-2026 Venue Details This will be an On-Phone Event. We’ll contact you using the phone number provided in your profile. RSVP now Before you RSVP, we need you to take care of a few things: 1. Create or update your job profile. Log in to your profile on Jobs at Apple and ensure your contact information is up to date. The primary email address on your profile should match the email address on this invitation. If you don’t have a job profile, this is your opportunity to create one. 2. Learn about Apple Retail. While you’re on Jobs at Apple, learn more about why people come to work at Apple. Read about our various roles and watch videos with real store employees — this is a great way to prepare for your phone appointment. 3. Register. Register for a convenient time to speak on the phone with a member of Apple’s hiring team. If you have any questions about registration or if the event is showing full, please reply back so we can provide assistance. RSVP now. 4. Joining the event. For virtual events, please start your webex link no earlier than 5 minutes before your scheduled session and plan to be with us for the entire duration. The link will be in your registration confirmation email or you can log on to your RSVP.apple.com to view the details. For on-site events, please arrive 15 minutes early on your reserved date and time, and plan to be with us for the entire duration. For on-phone events, we’ll contact you using the phone number provided. Feel free to dress business casual. This invitation will remain open for a limited time, so reserve your place before it’s too late. Registration deadline: 15-Jul-2026. If you’re unavailable for any of the times provided, please reply to this email. If you’re no longer interested in pursuing opportunities at Apple, please opt out to avoid receiving any further notifications about this event. Apple is committed to working with and providing reasonable accommodations to job applicants with physical or mental disabilities. Should you need any accommodations to participate in the hiring event, or if you have any other questions or concerns about the event, please reply to this email. We look forward to speaking with you soon. Regards, Apple www.apple.com/jobs/sg If you prefer not to receive emails from Apple regarding this event please click here Apple is an equal opportunity employer that is committed to inclusion and diversity. We seek to promote equal opportunity for all applicants without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, disability, Veteran status, or other legally protected characteristics. Copyright @ 2026 Apple Inc. One Apple Park Way, Cupertino, CA 95014 USA.

subject: US-Iran ceasefire teeters
body: Plus, Lindsey Graham dies aged 71 and Zelenskyy dismisses Ukraine’s prime minister ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Benjamin Wilhelm Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 13 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * US and Iran battle over Strait of Hormuz * Chinese regulators crack down on top ratings for corporate bonds * Partisan divisions spill over at US Supreme Court ‌ The US has launched its fifth round of strikes on Iran in the last week, as Washington and Tehran escalate hostilities over control of the Strait of Hormuz. What’s happening: American forces “began launching more strikes against Iran to continue degrading their ability to attack civilian mariners and commercial ships freely transiting the Strait of Hormuz”, US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said on Sunday. Centcom said the fresh round of strikes came after the IRGC fired at a commercial vessel and that US forces had intercepted an Iranian cruise missile and drone. The strikes followed an intense round of US attacks on Iran on Saturday night, which hit about 140 targets as a ceasefire between the warring parties came closer to collapse. The US attacks on Saturday were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps hitting a commercial ship transiting the strait and declaring the waterway closed. The US insisted on Sunday that it was open. Battle over Hormuz: Despite Iran’s declaration that the strait was closed, the US insisted on Sunday that it was open. The waterway “is open to all vessels seeking to lawfully transit the international waterway”, and that “pathways for free transit . . . remain open”, the US military said. “It’s open,” US President Donald Trump told NBC News about the strait on Sunday. “We bombed the hell out of them last night. They’re very, very evil and sick people.” Read the full story. * Analysis: After a week of escalating clashes with the US, Iran has taken a high-stakes gamble over the Strait of Hormuz. * Inside the risky race through the Strait of Hormuz: Vessels that dare to use the route close to Oman’s coast face increased risk of Iranian missiles. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: India releases June inflation figures. * Ukraine war: French President Emmanuel Macron hosts a meeting in Paris of the “coalition of the willing”, set up for European allies to discuss security guarantees for Kyiv. * Oil markets: Opec publishes its monthly oil report. WAS THIS FORWARDED TO YOU? If you’re an FT subscriber, sign up here to get this newsletter delivered straight to your inbox. If you’re new to the FT, take out a subscription here. Sent every weekday. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. Chinese regulators are pressuring rating agencies to cut back on triple-A designations for higher-interest borrowers amid mounting concern about assessments of creditworthiness in the country’s corporate bond market. The People’s Bank of China told domestic agencies in April to review high credit ratings, especially for bonds with much higher yields than government debt. 2. US senator Lindsey Graham, one of the most influential and hawkish Republicans in Congress, has died at the age of 71 after a brief illness. Graham represented South Carolina in Congress for more than 30 years and was standing for re-election in November’s midterms. He had returned from a trip to Ukraine shortly before his death, which occurred at his home in Washington. Read the full story. * Lindsey Graham obituary: The veteran proponent of US power was a Trump critic who became one of the president’s most influential advocates. 3. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that he will replace Ukraine’s prime minister and shake up his cabinet, in a sweeping government overhaul that he said was needed to deliver a new political strategy for the country. The reshuffle comes less than a year since the last shake-up and is the third since the full-scale war with Russia broke out in February 2022. 4. Former Qatari ruler Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, who oversaw the modernisation of the gas-rich Gulf state, has died aged 74. After ousting his father in a palace coup in 1995, Sheikh Hamad steered the transformation of Qatar into a global investor and an outsized actor in regional and international diplomacy, at times frustrating its Arab neighbours while garnering a reputation as a maverick. 5. Brussels is preparing to give itself new powers to fine Big Tech for failing to protect consumers and especially children from online spending traps as part of a bigger push to boost social media safeguards, the EU’s top justice official has said. KNIVES OUT AT THE US SUPREME COURT The members of the US Supreme Court © Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Justice Amy Coney Barrett has compared sitting on the US Supreme Court to “being in an arranged marriage with no option of divorce”. After a politically fraught term marred by infighting, its nine members may need couples therapy. Over the course of a term dominated by Trump’s controversial second-term agenda — from his immigration crackdown to his bureaucratic takeover — the knives have come out at the nation’s top court. In pointed remarks and fiery written opinions, its justices have traded barbs in a manner typically kept out of the public eye. The hardening of ideological lines at the once collegial top court could have profound consequences for public support of the nation’s third branch of government. US justice correspondent Ella Lee reports from Washington. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Goldilocks zone of messiness: Tourists flock to Japan to bask in the country’s orderliness, writes Leo Lewis. But has a refusal to tolerate chaos killed its capacity for risk? * China’s thriving ‘temple economy’: After decades of economic transformation and social change, a new generation is seeking answers in religion. * Vibe-coding: Our obsession with AI code-writing tools is overwhelming the web’s unsung human caretakers, writes Sam Learner for FT Magazine. CHART OF THE DAY Private equity’s biggest players are driving a fundraising revival that has left smaller firms trailing, with the market seized by a winner-takes-all dynamic. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Alex Bilmes estimates he has smoked about 250,000 cigarettes over 35 years: “Sometimes, even while I was smoking a cigarette, I was jonesing for the next one.” Writing for HTSI’s health and fitness issue, he explains how he finally managed to quit. © Peter Flude ‌ ‌ MARKETS AT 0604 GMT+8 INDICES Hang Seng ▲ +0.60% at 24,175 Nikkei 225 ▲ +1.20% at 68,558 S&P 500 ▲ +0.42% at 7,575 Eurofirst 300 ▲ +0.02% at 2,567 Nasdaq 100 ▲ +0.33% at 29,825 FTSE 100 ▲ +0.24% at 10,497 CURRENCIES € / $ ▼ -0.08% at 1.1404 $ / ¥ ▲ +0.02% at 161.7200 £ / $ ▼ -0.23% at 1.3376 € / £ ▲ +0.04% at 0.8516 COMMODITIES Brent Crude ▼ -1.04% at 75.22 WTI Crude Oil ▲ +0.14% at 71.51 Comex Gold ▼ -0.33% at 4,090.60 Copper ▼ -0.02% at 6.23 Natural Gas ▲ +0.27% at 2.95 10-YEAR BOND YIELDS US ▼ -0.008 at 4.561 UK ▲ 0.011 at 4.883 Japan ▼ -0.055 at 2.712 Bund ▲ 0.004 at 3.039 For the latest prices go to FT.com ‌ ‌ RECOMMENDED NEWSLETTERS FOR YOU One Must-Read Remarkable journalism you won’t want to miss. subject: Week Ahead: Burnham’s blessing
body: Britain’s next PM to be rubber-stamped while Wall Street lenders to roar ahead of the earnings season charge ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Jonathan Moules Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 12 2026 Former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham is expected to be anointed as Labour leader on Friday © AFP via Getty Images Hello and welcome to the working week. Or, if you are Andy Burnham, welcome to coronation week. The Greater Manchester mayor turned prime minister-in-waiting needs just one more Labour MP to formally endorse him and the keys to Number 10 are his. He has the backing of 322 MPs. One more, and no other candidate can secure the support of the 81 MPs needed to make a bid for the leadership. This point is expected to be reached after the doors of the Palace of Westminster open on Monday. Burnham is expected to be anointed as Labour leader on Friday and will then enter Downing Street as prime minister on July 20. The job of government will continue during this time, or at least that’s what (current) chancellor Rachel Reeves hopes. Her annual Mansion House speech on Tuesday, alongside remarks from Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, has been in the diary for a while. Some in the City of London think it makes more sense to postpone it, but sources close to the chancellor say it will take place even if it might be her last appearance as head of the Treasury. Reeves thinks she has some unfinished business. Perhaps it has something to do with the publication of the government’s financial services AI adoption plan, which will happen on the same day. The FT urges caution in this area. Wall Street bank earnings herald the arrival of what is set to be another blockbuster results season thanks to the rewards from listings such as those of SpaceX and SK Hynix, as well as the return of mega-mergers. The five largest US investment banks — JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and Citigroup — are forecast to report a year-on-year increase of 27 per cent in fees in the second quarter with a total of $11.1bn, according to estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Gains from fees from equity capital markets alone are predicted to total $2.5bn across the five banks, which would be the largest haul since 2021. One question for the banks, though, is how much surprise to the upside they can really deliver since quite a lot of this is priced in by now. Growth is a theme for the week, with a quarterly update from China and a monthly estimate from the UK, both hoping to surprise on the upside, perhaps thanks to the Iran war reboot arriving after the figures were compiled. Other data points and company earnings call dates are detailed below. ONE MORE THING . . . ‌ ‌ Thank you for the lido suggestions. Canary Wharf’s freshly opened swimming lanes are now on my to-do list, but will require the continuation of this summer’s fair weather. This week we might find out if it will hold up. Wednesday is St Swithin’s Day, a moment in English folklore when the weather is said to predict the forecast for the coming weeks. If it rains, you can expect 40 more days of rain; if the weather is fair, 40 days of sunshine typically follow. Here’s hoping for the latter, just a little cooler than it has been of late. Are you hot enough? Get in touch at jonathan.moules@ft.com or, if you are reading this from your inbox, hit reply. And have a good week. KEY ECONOMIC AND COMPANY REPORTS ‌ ‌ Here is a more complete list of what to expect in terms of company reports and economic data this week. MONDAY * Huw Pill, Bank of England chief economist, gives a speech at the International Finance and Banking Society conference at Bayes Business School in London * Ruth Smith, executive director of the Resolution Directorate at the Bank of England, gives a speech at UK Finance, a membership body for banking and finance firms * Opec monthly oil report * UK: National Audit Office publishes report on increasing construction skills, examining whether the government is well placed to secure value for money in delivering the construction skills required by employers. * Earnings calls: Grafton trading update, HCL Technologies Q1 TUESDAY * Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey faces questions from MPs on the Treasury Committee on financial stability following AI warnings * Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago head Austan Goolsbee takes part in a fireside chat at the Kenosha Area Business Alliance business lunch in Wisconsin * Arc Resources holds a special meeting of shareholders to vote on the proposed acquisition of the company by Shell * SpaceX set to launch its latest batch of Starlink satellites * China: June trade figures * India: June wholesale price index (WPI) inflation rate data * Switzerland: June producer price index (PPI) inflation rate data * UK: British Retail Consortium June Retail Sales Monitor * US: June real earnings and consumer price index (CPI) inflation rate data * Earnings calls: Bank of America Q2, BP Q2 trading statement, Citigroup Q2, Fastenal Q2, Goldman Sachs Q2, JPMorgan Chase Q2, The Watches of Switzerland FY, Wells Fargo Q2 WEDNESDAY * Bank of England executive director for prudential policy, David Bailey, speaks at the International Finance and Banking Society conference, hosted at Bayes Business School in London * Federal Reserve Bank of New York president John Williams speaks at the Partnership for New York City event * 20th anniversary of Twitter being launched to the public. The company has since been rebranded as X. Canada: interest rate announcement and monetary policy report * China: Q2 GDP estimate * France: June net foreign exchange reserves * US: Beige Book and June PPI inflation rate data * Earnings calls: ASML Q2, Barratt Redrow trading update, BlackRock Q2, B&M European Value Retail Q1 trading statement, BNY Q2, Cohort FY, Galliford Try trading update, Handelsbanken HY, JB Hunt Q2, Morgan Stanley Q2, M&T Bank Q2, PNC Financial Services Q2, Rio Tinto Q2 operations review (8.30am local time in Sydney), TomTom Q2 THURSDAY * Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas president Lorie Logan speaks at an event at the Houston branch of the bank as part of her “Listening in 360” tour * Italy: June CPI inflation rate data * South Korea: interest rate announcement * UK: May GDP estimate * US: July NAHB Housing Market Index * Earnings calls: ABB Q2, Abbott Laboratories Q2, Alcoa Q2, BHP FY operational review, Citizens Financial Group Q2, Crest Nicholson HY, DFS Furniture trading statement, Dunelm Q4 trading update, Essity Q2, Frasers FY, Intuitive Surgical Q2, Johnson & Johnson Q2, Manpower Q2, Netflix Q2, Ocado HY, Premier Foods Q1 trading update, Prologis Q2, Publicis Groupe HY, SSE Q1 trading statement, State Street Q2, Trustpilot trading update, TSMC Q2, United Airlines Q2, UnitedHealth Q2, US Bancorp Q2 FRIDAY * EU: June harmonised indices of consumer prices (HICP) inflation rate data * UK: June company insolvency figures * Earnings calls: Burberry Q1, Fifth Third Bancorp Q1, Sandvik Q2, Skanska Q2, Telia HY, Travelers Q2, Volvo Cars Q2 WORLD EVENTS ‌ ‌ Finally, here is a rundown of other events and milestones this week. MONDAY * Belgium: EU foreign ministers gather in Brussels for the Foreign Affairs Council. The agenda includes talks on Russia’s war against Ukraine, with Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiha joining for an informal exchange * UK: Centre for Cities hosts an online discussion with Sir Andy Street, former West Midlands mayor, examining the progress of devolution in England. Prospective prime minister Andy Burnham made further devolution a central message in a policy speech last month TUESDAY * France: Bastille Day, marking the start of the French Revolution with the storming of the Bastille prison in Paris in 1789. Events include a military parade in Paris attended by French President Emmanuel Macron * Kazakhstan: Roscosmos Soyuz MS-29 spacecraft launch, carrying Nasa astronaut Anil Menon and Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina to the International Space Station * UK: Chancellor Rachel Reeves and Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey deliver their annual Mansion House speeches at the event hosted by Lady Mayor of the City of London Dame Susan Langley at her official residence, Mansion House. The government’s financial services AI adoption plan will be officially launched at the event * US: Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh presents the semi-annual monetary policy report to the House committee on financial services WEDNESDAY * Brunei: Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, the longest-reigning living royal, celebrates his 80th birthday amid questions of succession due to his ailing health * Gibraltar: the EU and UK provisionally apply their post-Brexit border deal to the British territory * UK-India free trade agreement comes into force * US: attorney-general nominee Todd Blanche appears before the Senate judiciary committee at the start of a two-day confirmation hearing. THURSDAY * Thailand: British royals Princess Anne and her husband Sir Tim Laurence begin a two-day visit with education and cultural engagements planned * UK: Andy Burnham will prepare to enter Downing Street as the country’s new prime minister if nobody else has entered the Labour leadership contest by today’s deadline. Also, the House of Commons begins its summer recess FRIDAY * China: Shanghai hosts the 2026 world AI conference and high-level meeting on global AI governance, which runs until next Monday * UK: 131st BBC Proms season opens at the Royal Albert Hall in London SATURDAY * UK: Men’s Vitality Blast Finals Day of the T20 cricket tournament, including semi-finals and final in Birmingham * Uruguay: Constitution Day SUNDAY * São Tomé and Príncipe: presidential election * South Korea: 48th session of the World Heritage Committee begins in Busan * US: World Cup men’s football tournament final at the New York New Jersey Stadium ‌ ‌ Thanks for reading. subject: 📰 Iran closes the Strait
body: ---------- Hello, Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed and struck US bases and allies across the Gulf after Washington launched a third round of strikes this week, hitting 140 military targets. This comes as President Trump lashed out at NATO allies in Ankara, ordering a halt to trade with Spain, and as Germany unveiled a budget dedicating one in every five euros of federal spending to defence. Read more below ⤵️ -------------------- # **Top 5 Stories** 1️⃣ 🇩🇪[ Germany puts defence at centre of new budget](https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-ramps-up-defense-spending-in-new-budget-plan-ahead-of-nato-summit/): Chancellor Merz's cabinet approved a draft 2027 budget allocating €109.7bn, around one in every five euros of federal spending, to defence, with the share projected to reach nearly a third by 2030. Finance Minister Klingbeil said Germany "cannot defend ourselves against Putin with a balanced budget," while Chancellor Merz said Berlin is doubling its defence budget within four years after President Trump called its spending "Ridiculous!" 2️⃣ 🇵🇸[ Hamas dissolves its Gaza governing body](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20260706-hamas-dissolves-gaza-governing-body-clearing-way-for-technocratic-committee): Hamas announced the dissolution of the body that has governed Gaza for nearly two decades, clearing the way for the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza headed by Ali Shaath. A spokesman said the group stepped aside "to remove any pretexts for the occupation," though its disarmament remains unresolved and the committee has stayed outside Gaza for months, reportedly due to Israeli objections. 3️⃣ 🇷🇺[ Russia recasts Ukraine fight as a war with NATO](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/7/russia-touts-war-with-nato-amid-losses-in-ukraine): In televised remarks, President Putin and General Gerasimov attributed Ukraine's battlefield resilience to Western backing, with President Putin claiming his forces "completely liberated" Kostiantynivka and seized over 3,000 sq km this year, though the Institute for the Study of War puts actual gains since January at roughly 97 sq km. Ukrainian officials and analysts said the framing is meant to justify a prolonged war and a possible mobilisation after September's parliamentary vote. 4️⃣ 🇨🇺[ Cubans protest after third nationwide blackout](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20g0d3ry4o): Residents in several parts of the island banged pots to voice anger over the latest nationwide power cut, the third this year, which came on top of state-imposed rolling outages lasting up to 70 hours in rural areas. President Díaz-Canel acknowledged the discontent but urged Cubans to direct their anger at Washington, while the US ambassador to the UN blamed the Cuban government. 5️⃣ 🇪🇺[ EU court rejects Apple challenge to Big Tech rules](https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-court-knocks-down-apple-challenge-big-tech-rules/): The EU General Court dismissed Apple's challenge against its gatekeeper designation under the Digital Markets Act, confirming the designation for the App Store and iOS in full and ruling its iMessage challenges inadmissible. Apple said it believes the DMA "goes beyond what is lawful and proportionate" but declined to say whether it will appeal, with two other cases still pending. -------------------- # **Together with:** ### 200+ Claude Prompts Top Professionals Actually Use at Work View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/3d30de6f-31bf-4508-924e-795f6a3aa751/200%2B_Claude_Prompts_to_Supercharge_your_productivity.jpg?t=1776971303) Follow image link: (https://magic.beehiiv.com/v1/faa6a747-8c1c-43c1-8155-91aa43268f01?email=umairaamir.aziz@gmail.com&redirect_to=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.superhuman.ai%2Fforms%2F8e8ace74-9c29-42f8-8e52-2706d2a41454&utm_source=beehiiv&utm_campaign=NORKHDZXI9&redirect_delay=3&_bhiiv=opp_da466d1c-50e1-432f-b016-1e1afdc520d8_d22f5b49&bhcl_id=d10c03f6-5548-4b83-bd2a-6a4063d4809e_016ec938-29f5-4087-952a-b817dd00b4f7_b998e573-6d8b-4811-a222-4ba20eadbbe9) Caption: Claude can be your analyst, editor, and strategist. But most professionals are using it to fix grammar. These 200+ Claude prompts take it from grammar tool to your most powerful AI work assistant. Sign up for [Superhuman AI](https://magic.beehiiv.com/v1/faa6a747-8c1c-43c1-8155-91aa43268f01?email=umairaamir.aziz@gmail.com&redirect_to=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.superhuman.ai%2Fforms%2F8e8ace74-9c29-42f8-8e52-2706d2a41454&utm_source=beehiiv&utm_campaign=NORKHDZXI9&redirect_delay=3&_bhiiv=opp_da466d1c-50e1-432f-b016-1e1afdc520d8_d22f5b49&bhcl_id=d10c03f6-5548-4b83-bd2a-6a4063d4809e_016ec938-29f5-4087-952a-b817dd00b4f7_b998e573-6d8b-4811-a222-4ba20eadbbe9) and get: * 200+ ready-to-use Claude prompts to get real work done in minutes — researched, tested, and used by professionals at Google, Microsoft, and NASA * Superhuman AI newsletter (4 min daily) so you keep learning new AI tools and skills to stay ahead in your career — the prompts are just the beginning [Claim your free prompts](https://magic.beehiiv.com/v1/faa6a747-8c1c-43c1-8155-91aa43268f01?email=umairaamir.aziz@gmail.com&redirect_to=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.superhuman.ai%2Fforms%2F8e8ace74-9c29-42f8-8e52-2706d2a41454&utm_source=beehiiv&utm_campaign=NORKHDZXI9&redirect_delay=3&_bhiiv=opp_da466d1c-50e1-432f-b016-1e1afdc520d8_d22f5b49&bhcl_id=d10c03f6-5548-4b83-bd2a-6a4063d4809e_016ec938-29f5-4087-952a-b817dd00b4f7_b998e573-6d8b-4811-a222-4ba20eadbbe9) -------------------- # **Major Story** View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/5f72062f-c513-476d-8d63-2cc873500d16/Untitled-1.png?t=1783866819) Caption: 🇺🇸🇮🇷** Iran closes Hormuz as US strikes again** The US launched a third round of strikes this week,[ hitting 140 Iranian military targets](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj9gkpp0dkeo) after CENTCOM said the IRGC "blatantly attacked" a Cyprus-flagged vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing the crew to abandon ship with one member missing. Iran's Revolutionary Guard declared the strait closed until further notice and launched retaliatory attacks on a US base in Jordan, with the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain all responding to Iranian missiles and drones. The escalation follows attacks on three commercial tankers earlier in the week and US strikes that killed 17 people and injured 115, according to Iranian officials. New Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in his first public statement since his father's funeral, vowed vengeance as "the will of the nation," while President Trump warned the US would "decimate and destroy" Iran if it attempted to kill him. Washington says talks will continue, demanding Tehran publicly declare the strait open and pledge to stop firing on commercial ships. -------------------- # **Other News** 1️⃣ 🇪🇺🇷🇺[ EU narrows visa ban on Russian combatants](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/07/08/eu-narrows-ban-on-russian-combatants-to-appease-france-and-italy): A scaled-back version of the proposed ban limits it to short-stay visas and to those who directly took part in the fighting in Ukraine, after France and Italy pushed back on the broader measure covering any military role. The ban forms part of the EU's 21st sanctions package, which ambassadors aim to adopt by mid-July to avoid an automatic revision of the Russian oil price cap. 2️⃣ 🇲🇽🇺🇸[ Mexico to press criminal charges over deaths in US custody](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c802431ppreo): The Mexican government said it will file criminal complaints in the US over the deaths of 14 citizens in ICE custody and three more during arrest operations, with Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco pledging "forceful legal action." More than a thousand people protested in Houston after an ICE officer shot dead Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, with four Democratic lawmakers demanding an independent investigation. 3️⃣ 🇺🇸🇹🇷[ President Trump to lift Turkiye sanctions, weighs F-35 sales](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/7/trump-says-will-lift-sanctions-on-turkiye-consider-selling-f-35s): Meeting President Erdogan on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, President Trump said Washington would remove the CAATSA sanctions imposed after Ankara bought Russian S-400 systems in 2019, and that resuming F-35 fighter sales was something he would consider. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has pushed back against any sale, warning it could shift the Middle East's balance of power, while President Erdogan said he hoped for a favourable decision. 4️⃣ 🇺🇸[ President Trump lashes out at allies, orders Spain trade halt](https://www.timesofisrael.com/trump-lashes-out-at-allies-at-nato-summit-orders-trade-halt-with-wasted-cause-spain/): President Trump told the Ankara summit he was "very upset" with NATO over Greenland and members' refusal to help in the war with Iran, singling out Spain as a "terrible partner" and ordering Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to halt trade with Madrid over its defence spending. Prime Minister Sánchez's office said it was treating the remarks as "business as usual," noting that individual EU members cannot be singled out on trade. ----------[Let us grow your social media channels](http://horizonatlasmedia.com) |[ Support Us](https://www.patreon.com/cw/HorizonGeopolitics) If you like our newsletter, we also recommend these: [Exec Sum](https://www.execsum.co/subscribe?_bhba=bf2a95d9-83f2-40e3-a79e-83b720b4bd3c&utm_source=geopoliticsdaily.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=us-urges-iran-departures&_bhlid=dd5cd3e57518973cc6d16cabab3d82938ad61b5d) - A concise daily snapshot of what matters across markets, tech, and business, Exec Sum is a solid read. Collection of the National Museum of Singapore, National Heritage Board. Our cover story revisits https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC69b2cU7BWPbOsNcaC5ZilNDRCwye5UjQn6XD4M6gcia3Od06AuImTBijPydlfdcTYF11wkvZid21tP0oZS9MppJr-5RAxLiEdcHT8Jg Tang Dynasty City (formerly Tang Dynasty Village). Although largely forgotten today, it was a big thing in the press at one point in the 1990s. A unique combination of theme park and movie studio, the replica of Chang’an city promised to transport people back to the golden age of China’s Tang dynasty. Sadly, it failed to move anyone to visit the theme park, which had to shut down, but it was a brave attempt at doing something different. https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC7ByjJXplQfVVT9ZbiIlqwuHvN5eakbZUrHA0XnNtjUI7wyvWxZnLyJAOCwGvEH742NaVOgpg6xbHSY9E3gT822sdjaAqn71IDJ2p3PQ Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh experiencing the traditional way of preparing Chinese tea at Tea Chapter, 1989. Courtesy of Tea Chapter. Speaking of doing something different, it's interesting to see that https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC8DDpJmpEFFFQdoYNqy5ErGWTtRQ4AdlqUoSk3prFB9PyoYhBSSGQm2qPzSr9mH-2qqi_846tOzyMFnp8JP2YnRBrz-a-1URyHCCapxQ non-fiction graphic works are gaining ground in Singapore. Other Singapore stories in this issue include https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC9pMo3PLFRFnKuwOZmQf7jswtma4DhsicPTuNsr1ARM5XzdQYp8Vk7eLsLbJLnkjFRddg6qTXfLHTzx73Lb6-rUKZkTKPbkLE9Fz-t7Q Sengkang’s past as a fisheries port, musically inclined civilian https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC-Nc9B_K3erOdiUBufr4jq0b33ghayv9ROHfuirqM51KhWGLwDUSfSJLLyuvtzNESu-ojdqMfEnFWb6ObtpAn_x7We0ycjuPwiFLEnEg internees in Changi , https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdC_mwT1fK7NRWBM_DVJAEy_3niGsEnmxsJHV4snrJtckOUWTbJdcUcLT0sEtDpWwwdu2mR0o8wm4V10X7wb06Mdg6IdEmSJK5_MiLkVdQ tea culture in Singapore, the evolution of Singapore's https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdDAE4GnH0fqFn1_dDkT4ajqt82m9DHQFMovbbXmFVKK82DIdFwxCoPTYW_hhaiwFJveRSReC3qljRBvH9HbXRLkIuvjKAx-piyfb-ZGAg coat of arms , and https://click.experience.nlb.gov.sg/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5MzV9AA0AAAAAAK0CqdDB1S3EfVA6F6iL5Sd3CI_bVgC9nUYCPQb30B_lxfkCQyFCMg7zuQGD5FD-GDehkDn5yroBGoQ9ZYuboKYV8I2L1ahY4BioNwSkdCXKyw Lee Kuan Yew's account of the days leading up to 9 August 1965. subject: Are you following AI or actually using it?
body: Hi Umair! How’s it going?? 😊 Something I've been thinking about lately. There are two very different relationships you can have with AI right now. You can follow it. Or you can use it. Following AI looks like: reading every announcement, watching every breakdown video, knowing which model beats which on which benchmark, having opinions on every new release. Using AI looks like: opening a tool, working on a real problem, building something, getting a result. Both feel productive. Only one actually is. And I say this as someone who has definitely spent more time than I'd like to admit in the first camp. The pull toward following is real. The space moves fast. There's always something new. And staying informed feels responsible. But I've noticed that the weeks where I've made the most progress - on actual projects and outputs are the weeks where I consumed almost nothing and just built. Here's a simple way to check which mode you're in. At the end of this week, what will you have made, built, or shipped because of AI? If the answer is "nothing" but you've read a lot about it ,that's the signal. The goal isn't to know more about AI. It's to do more with it. subject: Are we still early?

body: Plus: How vibe coding is overwhelming the internet, and tropical nights come to Europe ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser David Hindley Researcher, FT Edit ‌ ‌ July 11 2026 Good morning, here is your weekend edition of FT Edit, with a selection of the best FT features and opinion. But first, your verdicts from the past week. England kicked off the week with an epic World Cup victory against Mexico. But just as big a talking point as the score was the question of whether you stayed up until 2am to watch it. The other hot-button issue was that of bathtubs in bedrooms, on which you were resoundingly firm. You were far more divided over weight-loss drugs . . . We ended the week with an FT scoop on Silicon Valley’s tech giants selling their AI models to Chinese groups blacklisted by the Pentagon — and a question over who should control access to these vastly powerful tools. But more interesting than the majority of you who said “regulators”, was the 12 per cent who answered “no one” . . . AND ONE FOR THE WEEKEND . . . Postcards are dying, writes Rebecca Rose. When did you last send one? body: ADD MONEY TO BRING YOUR BALANCE TO ZERO Hi Umair, Your SGD balance is still below zero. Please add money in the next 3 days to bring your balance above zero. You won't be able to spend using your Revolut account until you've resolved this negative balance. WHAT HAPPENS IF I DON'T ADD MONEY? If your balance is still below zero after 3 days, we may attempt to recover the amount by: * debiting the equivalent value from one of your other Revolut currency accounts * withdrawing funds from your Personal Pockets or Savings * charging the amount you owe from a stored card HOW DO I TOP UP MY ACCOUNT? In your Revolut app: 1. Go to Home on the bottom menu 2. Under your balance, tap Accounts 3. Select the account with the negative balance 4. Tap Add money and select the drop-down menu Then you can add money via one of the following methods: * Apple Pay and Google Pay * AutoPay * Bank transfer * Debit card WHERE CAN I GET HELP? If you have any questions about this, or if you're experiencing financial difficulties that impact your ability to bring your balance above zero, get in touch with us via our 24/7 in-app chat — we're happy to help. subject: Editor’s Choice: A wild week in US foreign policy
body: Plus, Le Pen and Farage’s gambles, the price of Palantir’s politics and a gentle guide to the wealth tax debate ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Roula Khalaf Editor ‌ ‌ July 11 2026 Hello from the FT newsroom in London where we’ve been following another wild week in US foreign policy. In the Donald Trump era, there’s a new type of Nato summit, one designed to satisfy the US president and prevent him from blowing up the alliance. In Ankara, the venue for the summit, Trump spoke too much, as he often does, and made all sorts of confusing statements, including repeating his obsession with controlling Greenland (which we thought had been settled), threatening to cut off trade with Spain (a new one for Trump), and referring to Iran as the Islamic republic of Japan (unclear why he picked Japan). European allies, however, could at least point to the fact that he seemed more supportive of Ukraine, which, in itself, is hardly surprising given that he likes winners and Kyiv is doing better on the battlefront. In our FT View, we summarised the summit as “a vintage carnival of Trumpian caprice”. Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the Nato summit in Ankara © Win McNamee/Getty Images MY CHOICES THIS WEEK ‌ ‌ 1. Marine Le Pen and Nigel Farage both face accusations of financial irregularities. On Tuesday both responded by putting themselves up for election. Our editorial board explains why — and what chance their strategies have of paying off. 2. We got the scoop that OpenAI and Google are selling their advanced AI models to Chinese tech giants blacklisted by the Pentagon, exposing a gap in Washington’s efforts to slow Beijing’s AI development. Read the full story. 3. The resumption of tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran this week coincided with the six-day funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening salvo of the war in February. Our Tehran correspondent explains what we can expect from his son and successor Mojtaba Khamenei. 4. Our reporters reveal that Tesco is exploring a sale of its central and eastern European operations. The move would bring down the curtain on a three-decade attempt by the UK’s biggest supermarket to build a global retail empire. 5. Tech group Palantir’s enthusiastic embrace of Trump’s policies and its defence of Israel’s war in Gaza have spurred outrage in the US and Europe. Here’s how the tech group’s politics could threaten the core of its $330bn business. 6. After two decades of near stagnation, economic growth has become Britain’s number one priority. Can incoming prime minister Andy Burnham get the country growing again? Our chief economics commentator Martin Wolf is sceptical. 7. Wall Street’s boutique investment banks insisted multimillion-dollar guaranteed payouts for star bankers were a temporary phenomenon. But the windfalls look like they are here to stay, while an upswing in revenues is yet to materialise. 8. The debate surrounding wealth taxes can be harsh. So as Californians gear up to vote on a 5 per cent tax on billionaires’ wealth, FT columnist Soumaya Keynes offers a gentle guide to the key arguments for, against and in between. 9. Transformers are fundamental to the flow of electricity. But the most powerful ones are facing bottlenecks, driving up prices and jeopardising the relentless race for AI expansion. This visual story breaks down everything you need to know about the century-old device choking the world’s AI push. 10. Professor Emily Wilson is something of a rock star in her field. Her 2017 translation of The Odyssey — the first by a woman in English verse — helped to inspire Christopher Nolan’s new film. In this week’s Lunch with the FT, Wilson talks to our foreign editor Alec Russell about the resonance of Homer’s epics. WHAT TO LISTEN TO ‌ ‌ In 1720, the South Sea Company was one of the most valuable businesses in Britain until a spectacular collapse in its publicly traded shares triggered the country’s first major stock market crisis. On the latest episode of The Story of Money, hosts Robin Wigglesworth and Gillian Tett speak to Professor Thomas Levenson about the speculation and financial engineering that inflated the South Sea Bubble — and how its dramatic fallout helped reshape modern finance.
